items.ig_caption:
4,972 chatbot messages. All of them said "hello". 👋

What Expert Insights reported (5 Nov), citing Era's research:
→ Era ran seven Flowise honeypots from July to October; every stored user message was "hello" and the bot replies held command output
→ A Chinese-language framework Era calls "Greeter" exploited CVE-2024-58351, an old critical Flowise flaw, to run commands without changing the saved chatflow
→ It probed AWS, Azure and Google Cloud metadata services and searched for SSH keys and Flowise's encryption key (the honeypot credentials were fake)
→ Commands came 3.5 seconds apart; Era says that suggests automation, possibly an AI agent, but timing alone can't prove it
→ Shodan shows 4,372 Flowise instances exposed; Era says 703 had no authentication

What to do: update Flowise, require authentication on its APIs, run it as non-root, and give it a narrowly scoped cloud identity with no long-lived keys in files.

cover.hook: Someone broke into a chatbot platform. Botpress says they wanted the AI credits.
cover.sub: An intruder read bot configs in 16 customer workspaces with a staff API credential.

slides.title: How they got in
slides.body: Botpress says probing of an internal authentication proxy began on 12 Oct. A flaw in its sign-in validation gave access from 13 to 21 Oct. It found no sign that an employee's identity-provider account was compromised.

slides.label: on 21 Oct (07:44–08:23 UTC): a staff API credential read bot configs in 16 customer workspaces
slides.note: Integration settings were also changed in two other workspaces

slides.title: Why bot configs matter
slides.body: Bot configurations can hold third-party credentials: AI provider API keys, messaging-channel tokens and CRM logins. Botpress says the goal was AI usage to resell on AI black markets.

slides.title: What Botpress says wasn't hit
slides.body: No ransom demand, no sign data was published or sold, no changes to source code, build pipelines or packages, no access to end-user conversations. Fixed 21 Oct; attempts through 3 Nov were rejected.

slides.title: Do this week
items: If notified: treat every credential in the affected bots as exposed and rotate it
List every platform that stores a copy of your AI API keys
Set spend alerts on AI provider keys so resold usage shows up fast
Vendors: review staff admin access into customer workspaces

items.x_text:
Claude Code "don't ask again": Apiiro found 1,122 public .claude/settings.local.json files holding secrets, and 2,539 distinct secrets across 1,994 repos when history and transcripts are included. Rotate first, then .gitignore.

#AISecurity #InfoSec
items.ig_caption:
2,539 secrets. Saved by "don't ask again". 🔑

What iTWire (7 Nov) and SecurityOnline (8 Nov) reported from Apiiro's research:
→ Choosing "Yes, and don't ask again" can make Claude Code save the full approved shell command, credentials included, in .claude/settings.local.json
→ Of 104,185 public copies of that file, 1,122 held secrets (1,379 distinct values)
→ Counting Git history, shared settings and agent transcripts: 2,539 distinct secrets across 1,994 repositories
→ Among them, per SecurityOnline: 379 database passwords, 149 AI model API keys and 43 SSH server logins; gitleaks and TruffleHog together missed 215 of the files
→ Apiiro didn't test the keys, but notified 63 organisations on 2–3 Nov; one confirmed its exposed key was live

What to do: search your repos for .claude/settings.local.json, rotate anything in it first, then untrack it and add it to .gitignore. Deleting the file doesn't remove old commits, forks or clones. Use environment variables instead of typing raw passwords into commands.

cover.hook: Name. Home address. Card number. Linked crypto wallets.
cover.sub: Gnosis Pay confirmed a breach of its legacy card system. One affected user listed what was exposed.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: Gnosis Pay says an unauthorized party accessed the legacy system behind its Gnosis Pay-branded cards. It detected the access on 3 Nov, began containment within two hours and confirmed the breach on 6 Nov.

slides.title: What leaked
slides.body: Gnosis Pay hasn't said how many customers were affected or published a full list of exposed data. Rotki founder Lefteris Karapetsas said his full name, home address, card number and linked wallet addresses were exposed.

slides.label: from detection (3 Nov) to the start of containment, per Gnosis Pay
slides.note: The breached system was already due to retire on 20 Dec 2026

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: A home address tied to wallet addresses makes targeted phishing easier. Gnosis Pay says customer funds were not affected and its white-label enterprise platform was not hit. It made 3D Secure mandatory for online payments.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Expect phishing about Gnosis Pay, partner apps or your card
Never share a seed phrase, private key, PIN or full card number
Watch card and wallet activity closely
Retiring a system? Keep it monitored until it's switched off
